Performance

Source: vignettes/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd

This article reports what zurand costs and how that was measured. The code below is not run when the vignette is built: a fair benchmark takes minutes and needs every competing package installed.

Results

Millions of values per second for n = 1e7, median of five rounds, from the package’s benchmark workflow: on a GitHub-hosted runner for Linux (2026-09-26), and the workflow’s code run locally on an Apple M1 (2026-09-27).

Linux x86_64, 1 thread Linux x86_64, 4 threads Apple M1, 1 thread Apple M1, 8 threads
uniform
zurand (xoshiro256pp) 864 1801 2196 4984
zurand (philox4x64) 276 594 574 2404
randompack (x256++simd) 688 684 1918 1888
randompack (philox) 252 252 574 572
dqrng 368 367 311 310
base R runif() 104 104 213 210
normal
zurand (xoshiro256pp) 366 919 739 3143
zurand (philox4x64) 215 501 377 1622
randompack (x256++simd) 355 355 718 708
randompack (philox) 184 184 375 369
RcppZiggurat (MT) 125 124 225 221
dqrng 143 143 235 233
base R rnorm() 28 28 43 42
  • Linux: AMD EPYC 7763, 4 cores, AVX2, OpenMP.
  • Apple M1: a MacBook Air (fanless), 8 cores (4 performance and 4 efficiency), 16 GB, NEON, on mains power, with OpenMP through the runtime R ships (see Threads). Not a CI runner: GitHub’s M1 runner is a virtualised 3-core slice whose numbers moved by a third between runs (1364-1837 M/s uniform on one thread).

Reading the table

  • Against dqrng and RcppZiggurat, zurand’s default engine is 2.3-7x faster on uniform and 2.9-3.3x on normal, single-threaded.
  • Against randompack’s SIMD engine, the fastest single-threaded competitor, zurand leads on every row. Uniform: 1.26x on x86_64, and 1.15x on the M1 for fills of 1e6 and 1e7 values (0.97x for 1e5, a fill small enough to stay in cache; same-machine A/B, one thread). Normal: 1.03x on this Zen 3, 1.08x on a Xeon 6973P (the same-machine A/B behind #43) and 1.01-1.03x on the M1, where method = "mcfarland" (below) is 1.09x. Both vectorise the generator (AVX2 on x86_64, NEON on arm64), and both use NumPy’s ziggurat, scalar, for normals; zurand’s takes the sign from a signed table, is unrolled by four, and keeps its rare slow path as plain out-of-line code.
  • With threads, zurand is the only package here that parallelizes at the R level, and the threaded output is bit-identical to the serial one. On four EPYC cores it is 2.6x randompack on both. On the M1’s eight it is 2.6x on uniform and 4.4x on normal: normals scale to 4.3x one thread, while uniform stops at about 2.3x, where it is writing 40 GB/s. Half of the M1’s cores are efficiency cores, and all eight still beat the four performance cores alone, by 4-13% on normals, so leave rng_threads() uncapped there.
  • The engines differ in speed, not in guarantees. Philox and Threefry are counter-based: each value is computed from its position. The default xoshiro256pp reseeds a cheap recurrence from Philox every 512 values.

What was tried and rejected

  • Non-temporal stores for large uniform fills: faster in a synthetic harness, slower at the R level on both Intel and AMD, one thread and four. R’s fresh vectors cost page faults, which streaming stores do not avoid.
  • A vectorised ziggurat fast path for normals: with AVX2 gathers it was 1.8x slower on Intel CPUs carrying the “Downfall” microcode fix; with plain loads it gained up to 9% on some Intel CPUs, nothing on AMD, and lost 6% for philox on another. The table lookups, not the arithmetic, are the cost.
  • Other ziggurat restructurings, all bit-identical: branch-free with a fix-up pass (1.4-1.6x slower; the ~1% reject branch is nearly free), randompack’s in-place structure, a packed {ki, wi} table (both tables already sit in L1 cache), and computing the rejected draws’ retry blocks four at a time (+2% for xoshiro, but 2% slower for threefry). What did pay was fewer instructions per draw: the sign folded into a signed table and the loop unrolled by four. The ziggurat’s implementation is now frozen; a faster Gaussian would be a different method.
  • Fusing the generator with the ziggurat transform, so no word buffer exists: slower on every CPU tried (i5, Zen 3, Zen 4, Xeon 6973P), by 12-95%. The 32 KiB buffer costs nothing; the transform is the cost.
  • Non-temporal stores, again, this time on freshly allocated memory with R’s 16-byte alignment: 1.3-3.3x slower than ordinary stores on every CPU. Closed.
  • Pre-faulting the output (MADV_POPULATE_WRITE): no gain. The page size is what matters; see Page size on Linux below.
  • Vectorised Box-Muller (VectorizedRNG.jl’s approach), made reproducible by evaluating log, sin and cos without fused multiply-add, so every vector lane and platform agrees with the scalar path. It was 3.5-13x slower per value than McFarland’s method on every CPU tried; allowing fused multiply-add gained at most 1.33x and changed 7% of values in the last bits. A divide, a square root and two polynomials cost more than one table load.
  • DC ZVA for normals on Apple Silicon. It is what lets zurand’s uniform fill beat randompack there, because that fill writes ten interleaved streams. Normals write one sequential stream, which the core already handles, and zeroing first made them slower.

Method

Every number comes from one protocol:

  • an -O2 build, never devtools::load_all() in its default debug mode, which compiles -O0 and runs about ten times slower;
  • every package measured in the same bench::mark() call on the same machine, and the ratio reported over repeated rounds, because absolute throughput on a shared machine moves by more than the differences being measured;
  • each competitor on its fastest engine, with its counter-based engine alongside where it has one.
library(zurand)
library(bench)

n <- 1e7
key <- rng_key(42L)                  # xoshiro256pp, the default
rp <- randompack::randompack_rng()   # randompack's fastest engine

rng_threads(1L)
bench::mark(
  zurand     = rng_uniform(key, n),
  randompack = rp$unif(len = n),
  dqrng      = dqrng::dqrunif(n),
  base       = runif(n),
  check = FALSE, min_iterations = 10
)

The full comparison is tools/benchmark.R in the source repository, and the benchmark workflow runs it on any GitHub-hosted runner.

Threads

rng_threads() caps how many threads zurand uses. The cap changes speed, never values:

key <- rng_key(1L)
rng_threads(1L); one <- rng_normal(key, 1e7)
rng_threads(0L); all <- rng_normal(key, 1e7)   # 0 removes the cap
identical(one, all)
#> [1] TRUE

Fills go parallel above 32,768 values. With several keys the threads split the keys; with one key they split its positions.

On macOS R does not set OpenMP compiler flags, so the package’s configure script tries the OpenMP runtime that R itself ships (libomp.dylib in R.home("lib"), see https://mac.r-project.org/openmp/), the same route data.table’s CRAN binaries take. It needs the OpenMP headers at build time, which CRAN’s build machines have; without them the build is single-threaded, and rng_threads() reports 1.

Two normal methods

rng_normal() has a second method, McFarland’s (2016) modified ziggurat, selected with method = "mcfarland". Its common case (253 draws in 256) uses the word’s low byte as the layer and returns X[i] * (the word as a signed integer). That needs no table comparison, and the sign comes free. It is about 8 instructions per value where the NumPy-table ziggurat needs 13. One thread, default engine, M/s relative to the default method in the same bench::mark() call:

1e5 1e6 1e7
EPYC 7763 (Zen 3) 1.08 1.15 1.17
EPYC 9V74 (Zen 4) 1.07 1.16 1.25
Neoverse N2 1.04 1.07 1.10
Apple M1 1.09 1.09 1.08

The default stays the NumPy-table ziggurat: changing it would change every existing normal stream. The two methods are separate streams: the same key gives unrelated values under each.

Page size on Linux

R serves a large vector from malloc(), which glibc maps fresh, so the fill is the first touch of every page and pays one page fault per page. With 4 KiB pages that costs more than generating the values. On the CI runner’s kernel, which uses 2 MiB pages for everything (transparent_hugepage/enabled = always), forcing 4 KiB pages took the uniform fill of 1e7 values from 837 to 242 M/s and the normal fill from 338 to 162. Kernels in madvise mode – the Ubuntu default – give a mapping 2 MiB pages only when asked, and zurand asks, on output vectors of 4 MiB and more (options(zurand.hugepages = FALSE) stops it). On the ubuntu-24.04-arm runner, a Neoverse N2 in madvise mode, one thread:

M/s, n = 1e7 zurand without the request zurand with it randompack
uniform 268 532 271
normal 214 344 200

No value changes; the kernel only tags the mapping. In always mode the request is skipped: the pages are already large, and asking explicitly also opts the mapping into synchronous compaction, measured 6-9% slower. macOS has no equivalent for memory it did not map itself.

Beyond R

The C API in zurand.h fills buffers the caller owns, from the caller’s own threads, with the values the R functions return. For a simulation that consumes random numbers as it goes, filling a reused buffer avoids allocating a new R vector per call. For large vectors that allocation is a large share of the time: on the Linux runner, allocating and zeroing a vector of 1e7 doubles alone runs at about 1,250 M/s, the same order as zurand’s four-thread fill.
